chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Nuh ibn Shu'ayb, from Shihab ibn 'Abd Rabbih, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), peace be upon him, said:

I asked him about the one in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) who washes the deceased, or the one who washes a deceased person, whether it is permissible for him to go to his wife and then perform the major ritual bath (ghusl). He said: 'It is the same; there is no problem with that. If he is in a state of major impurity, he washes his hands, performs ablution (wudu), and washes the deceased. So if he washes the deceased, then performs ablution, then goes to his wife, one washing (ghusl) suffices for him for both.'

key_terms.الْجُنُبِ: One in a state of major ritual impurity requiring a full bath
key_terms.يَغْتَسِلَ: To perform the major ritual bath (ghusl)

ai.seo_question: What are the ritual purity requirements for someone in a state of major impurity who washes a deceased body?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a person in the state of *junub* may wash the deceased without prior full ritual bath, requiring only hand washing and ablution, reflecting the practical flexibility in Shia fiqh for those performing funeral rites. The hadith further establishes the principle of *jama'* (combination) of impurities, where a single *ghusl* suffices for both the state of *junub* and the impurity incurred from washing the dead, provided the sequence is maintained. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on ease (*taysir*) in ritual purity obligations during communal duties.
